warmup.q: quotePayoutFee(amount) reads a global FeeConfig.rates and LocalTime.now(). A test calls quotePayoutFee(BigDecimal("200.00")) and expects 3.00. It passes on your laptop at 10:00. What can make the same test fail with no code change?
options: Only a JDK upgrade that changes how BigDecimal rounds
The time of day the build runs, and the order the tests run in
Only running the test class twice in a row
warmup.why: The function has two inputs that are not in its parameter list: the clock and the global. The test controls only the argument. At 17:00 in the nightly build, the late surcharge appears. After a test that set a premium rate and forgot to reset it, the percentage is different. A function whose every input is a parameter can't fail this way.

sections.h: This fee function has three inputs, and only one is a parameter
sections.html:
Here is a payout fee calculator. Something like it lives in every payments service.

Java
static BigDecimal quotePayoutFee(BigDecimal amount) {
    FeeRates rates = FeeConfig.rates;                  // a global that an admin endpoint can change
    LocalTime now = LocalTime.now();                   // the wall clock
    BigDecimal fee = amount.multiply(rates.percent()).setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN);
    if (fee.compareTo(rates.minimum()) < 0) fee = rates.minimum();
    if (!now.isBefore(rates.cutoff())) fee = fee.add(rates.lateSurcharge());
    audit.info("payout fee " + fee + " on " + amount + " at " + now);
    return fee;
}
Kotlin
fun quotePayoutFee(amount: BigDecimal): BigDecimal {
    val rates = FeeConfig.rates                        // a global that an admin endpoint can change
    val now = LocalTime.now()                          // the wall clock
    var fee = amount.multiply(rates.percent).setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN)
    if (fee < rates.minimum) fee = rates.minimum
    if (!now.isBefore(rates.cutoff)) fee += rates.lateSurcharge
    audit.info("payout fee $fee on $amount at $now")
    return fee
}

The signature says it takes an amount and returns a fee. That isn't the whole truth. It also takes the current time and whatever FeeConfig.rates holds at that moment, and it writes to the audit log. Those two inputs and that one output are hidden. You can't see them at the call site, and a test can't pass them in.

So every test of it is fragile. assertEquals(new BigDecimal("3.00"), quotePayoutFee(new BigDecimal("200.00"))) passes at 10:00 on your laptop. The nightly build runs at 17:00, after the 16:00 cut-off, and gets 4.00. Another test sets a premium merchant's rate on FeeConfig and forgets to put it back, and now your test fails only when JUnit happens to run that one first. And every call writes a real audit line, so a test that wants to check it has to capture logging output.

The usual fixes add machinery. You inject a Clock and pass Clock.fixed(...) in tests. You reset FeeConfig in @BeforeEach. You install a log appender. All of that works. All of it exists only because the function reaches outside its own parameters.

There is a simpler fix: make every input a parameter, and make the return value the only output. The rest of this lesson shows why that one change pays off so much.

try.title: Two tests, one global
steps: Open OrderDependentTests.kt (or its Java twin, OrderDependentTestsJava.java). It runs two little tests that share one global rate. Both pass in the order they are written. Predict what happens if you swap the order.
Run it with the command below. Then run it again with -Pargs=reverse added.
Find the line that makes standardFee fail. Notice that it isn't in standardFeeTest.

code.title: OrderDependentTests.kt
code.html: package workbench.functional.l01.demo import java.math.BigDecimal import java.math.RoundingMode // A global the fee function reads. An admin endpoint, or a test, can change it at any time. object Config { var percent = BigDecimal("0.015") } // Looks harmless. But its answer depends on something that is not in its parameter list. fun feeFor(amount: BigDecimal): BigDecimal = amount.multiply(Config.percent).setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN) // Two little "tests". The second sets up a premium merchant and never puts the global back. fun standardFeeTest(): String { val fee = feeFor(BigDecimal("200.00")) return if (fee == BigDecimal("3.00")) "pass" else "FAIL (expected 3.00, got $fee)" } fun premiumMerchantTest(): String { Config.percent = BigDecimal("0.025") val fee = feeFor(BigDecimal("200.00")) return if (fee == BigDecimal("5.00")) "pass" else "FAIL (expected 5.00, got $fee)" } fun main(args: Array<String>) { val tests = listOf("standardFee" to ::standardFeeTest, "premiumMerchant" to ::premiumMerchantTest) val order = if (args.firstOrNull() == "reverse") tests.reversed() else tests for ((name, test) in order) println("$name: ${test()}") }

But its answer depends on something that is not in its parameter list. static BigDecimal feeFor(BigDecimal amount) { return amount.multiply(percent).setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN); } static String standardFeeTest() { BigDecimal fee = feeFor(new BigDecimal("200.00")); return fee.equals(new BigDecimal("3.00")) ? "pass" : "FAIL (expected 3.00, got " + fee + ")"; } // Sets up a premium merchant and never puts the global back. static String premiumMerchantTest() { percent = new BigDecimal("0.025"); BigDecimal fee = feeFor(new BigDecimal("200.00")); return fee.equals(new BigDecimal("5.00")) ? "pass" : "FAIL (expected 5.00, got " + fee + ")"; } public static void main(String[] args) { List<Map.Entry<String, Supplier<String>>> tests = new ArrayList<>(List.of( Map.entry("standardFee", OrderDependentTestsJava::standardFeeTest), Map.entry("premiumMerchant", OrderDependentTestsJava::premiumMerchantTest))); if (args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("reverse")) Collections.reverse(tests); for (var t : tests) System.out.println(t.getKey() + ": " + t.getValue().get()); } }

try.expect: In the written order both tests print pass. Reversed, premiumMerchant still passes, but standardFee prints FAIL (expected 3.00, got 5.00). The cause is in the other test, which set Config.percent and never reset it. feeFor can't protect itself, because the rate is not one of its inputs.

sections.h: A pure function depends only on its arguments and changes nothing
sections.html:
A pure function follows two rules. Its result depends only on its arguments, so two calls with the same values give the same answer. And calling it changes nothing outside it. Break either rule and the function is impure.

Anything a call does besides hand back its value is a side effect: writing a database row, charging a card, sending a Kafka message, logging, changing a field or the contents of a parameter. The first rule has a half that people forget. Reading something that can change also breaks purity: LocalTime.now(), Random.nextInt(), a mutable global, a cache that another thread fills. These are hidden inputs. The answer depends on them, so the same arguments can give different answers.

Here is the fee rule with every input moved into the parameter list:

Java
static BigDecimal payoutFee(BigDecimal amount, FeeRates rates, LocalTime requestedAt) {
    BigDecimal base = amount.multiply(rates.percent()).setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN);
    BigDecimal atLeastMinimum = base.max(rates.minimum());
    boolean late = !requestedAt.isBefore(rates.cutoff());
    return late ? atLeastMinimum.add(rates.lateSurcharge()) : atLeastMinimum;
}
Kotlin
fun payoutFee(amount: BigDecimal, rates: FeeRates, requestedAt: LocalTime): BigDecimal {
    val base = amount.multiply(rates.percent).setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN)
    val atLeastMinimum = base.max(rates.minimum)
    val late = !requestedAt.isBefore(rates.cutoff)
    return if (late) atLeastMinimum + rates.lateSurcharge else atLeastMinimum
}

FeeRates is a record in Java and a data class with vals in Kotlin, so it's a plain value that can't change under you. The time arrives as a LocalTime value, not as a clock to ask. Nothing gets logged. Now the test:

Java
assertEquals(new BigDecimal("4.00"), payoutFee(new BigDecimal("200.00"), STANDARD, LocalTime.of(16, 0)));
Kotlin
assertEquals(BigDecimal("4.00"), payoutFee(BigDecimal("200.00"), STANDARD, LocalTime.of(16, 0)))

No fake clock, no reset, no mocks. You can test 15:59:59 and 16:00 in two lines, run the tests in any order, and run them on eight threads at once. Nothing is shared, so nothing can race.

Purity is a property of what a function does, not of the language. Kotlin has no pure keyword, and neither compiler checks it. The clues are in the signature: plain value parameters, a real return type instead of Unit or void, and no clock, repository or logger among the dependencies.

try.title: Pure or not?
steps: For each function, decide pure or impure. For the impure ones, name the hidden input or the side effect. Write your answers down before you read the expected result.
1: fun vat(cents: Long) = cents * VAT_PERCENT / 100, where VAT_PERCENT is a const val.
2: fun isExpired(card: Card) = card.expiry < YearMonth.now().
3: fun total(lines: MutableList<Line>): Long { lines.sortBy { it.sku }; return lines.sumOf { it.cents } }.
4: fun newIdempotencyKey() = UUID.randomUUID().toString().
5: fun maskPan(pan: String) = "**** " + pan.takeLast(4).
6: fun fee(cents: Long): Long { metrics.counter("fee.calls").increment(); return cents * 15 / 1000 }.
try.expect: Pure: 1 (a const val can never change) and 5. Impure: 2 reads the clock, a hidden input. 3 sorts the caller's list in place, a side effect the caller can see, even though the sum is right. 4 reads a random source, so two calls never agree. 6 returns the right fee but bumps a counter on every call, a side effect. If you hesitated on 3, that's the one that bites in practice: the caller's list comes back reordered.

sections.h: Replace the call with its value
sections.html:
Pure functions have a property with a long name and a simple meaning. Referential transparency means you can replace a call with the value it returns, and the program does exactly the same thing.

Java
long total = fee(20_000) + fee(20_000);
long f = fee(20_000);
long same = f + f;                        // always equal to total
Kotlin
val total = fee(20_000) + fee(20_000)
val f = fee(20_000)
val same = f + f                          // always equal to total

You make this kind of change every day without thinking about it: extract a variable, inline a variable, move a call out of a loop. It's only safe when the call is pure. Try the same move on a call with a side effect:

Java
String c = provider.charge(card, 20_000);
List<String> receipts = List.of(c, c);                        // one charge
List<String> inlined = List.of(provider.charge(card, 20_000),
                               provider.charge(card, 20_000)); // two charges
Kotlin
val c = provider.charge(card, 20_000)
val receipts = listOf(c, c)                                    // one charge
val inlined = listOf(provider.charge(card, 20_000),
                     provider.charge(card, 20_000))            // two charges

Inlining the variable charged the customer twice. Nothing in the syntax warned you. Both versions look like the same expression, and only what you know about charge tells them apart.

That is what purity buys you in practice: the call site tells you everything. You can reorder pure calls, because no call depends on another one's effects. You can cache the result, because the same arguments always give the same answer (lesson 3 of this track builds memoize on exactly this). You can retry after a timeout, because a second call can't do anything twice. You can run it on many threads, because it touches nothing shared. With an impure function, each of those moves first needs you to read its body, and often the bodies of everything it calls.

try.title: One charge or two
steps: Run ReplaceTheCall (or ReplaceTheCallJava). Before you read the output, predict how many times the fake provider is called in each half.
Add println("computing fee") as the first line of fee (in Java, System.out.println(...)). Predict how many times it prints, then run again.
Is fee still pure? Decide before you read the expected result.

code.title: ReplaceTheCall.kt
code.html: package workbench.functional.l01.demo // Pure: the result depends only on the argument, and calling it changes nothing. fun fee(amountCents: Long): Long = amountCents * 15 / 1000 // Impure: charging a card is the whole point of the call. This fake provider counts the calls. object FakeProvider { var calls = 0 fun charge(cardToken: String, amountCents: Long): String { calls++ return "ch_$calls" } } fun main() { // 1. With a pure function, a call and its value are interchangeable. val f = fee(20_000) println("fee(20000) + fee(20000) = ${fee(20_000) + fee(20_000)}") println("val f = fee(20000); f + f = ${f + f}") // 2. The same "harmless" refactoring on an impure call changes what the program does. val c = FakeProvider.charge("tok_visa", 20_000) println("val c = charge(..); listOf(c, c) -> ${listOf(c, c)}, provider calls: ${FakeProvider.calls}") FakeProvider.calls = 0 val both = listOf(FakeProvider.charge("tok_visa", 20_000), FakeProvider.charge("tok_visa", 20_000)) println("listOf(charge(..), charge(..)) -> $both, provider calls: ${FakeProvider.calls}") }

alt.title: ReplaceTheCallJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.functional.l01.demo; import java.util.List; /** Java twin of ReplaceTheCall.kt: swapping a call for its value is safe only when the call is pure. */ public class ReplaceTheCallJava { // Pure: the result depends only on the argument, and calling it changes nothing. static long fee(long amountCents) { return amountCents * 15 / 1000; } // Impure: charging a card is the whole point of the call. This fake provider counts the calls. static int calls = 0; static String charge(String cardToken, long amountCents) { calls++; return "ch_" + calls; } public static void main(String[] args) { // 1. With a pure function, a call and its value are interchangeable. long f = fee(20_000); System.out.println("fee(20000) + fee(20000) = " + (fee(20_000) + fee(20_000))); System.out.println("long f = fee(20000); f + f = " + (f + f)); // 2. The same "harmless" refactoring on an impure call changes what the program does. String c = charge("tok_visa", 20_000); System.out.println("String c = charge(..); List.of(c, c) -> " + List.of(c, c) + ", provider calls: " + calls); calls = 0; List<String> both = List.of(charge("tok_visa", 20_000), charge("tok_visa", 20_000)); System.out.println("List.of(charge(..), charge(..)) -> " + both + ", provider calls: " + calls); } }

try.expect: The pure half prints 600 twice. The charge half shows one provider call for listOf(c, c), which holds the same receipt twice, and two calls for the inlined version, [ch_1, ch_2]. After you add the print, computing fee appears three times: once for val f, twice for fee(20000) + fee(20000). Printing is a side effect, so fee is no longer strictly pure: inlining f would now change the output. A debug print is harmless, but it is the same mechanism as the double charge.

sections.h: In Kotlin, if, when and try are expressions
sections.html:
Pure code computes values instead of changing variables. Kotlin helps more than Java here, because if, when and try are expressions: they produce a value that you can assign or return. In Java, if and try are statements. They do something, and produce nothing.

This is the habit both languages allow, a variable declared first and assigned in branches:

Java
AuthStatus status;
if (httpCode == 200) status = AuthStatus.APPROVED;
else if (httpCode == 402) status = AuthStatus.DECLINED;
else status = AuthStatus.ERROR;
Kotlin
var status: AuthStatus
if (httpCode == 200) status = AuthStatus.APPROVED
else if (httpCode == 402) status = AuthStatus.DECLINED
else status = AuthStatus.ERROR

And this is the expression form:

Java
AuthStatus status = switch (httpCode) {       // switch expression, JDK 14
    case 200 -> AuthStatus.APPROVED;
    case 402 -> AuthStatus.DECLINED;
    default -> AuthStatus.ERROR;
};
Kotlin
val status = when (httpCode) {
    200 -> AuthStatus.APPROVED
    402 -> AuthStatus.DECLINED
    else -> AuthStatus.ERROR
}

The expression version is a val, so nothing can reassign it later. It also can't be left without a value. Delete the else branch and Kotlin refuses to compile it: 'when' expression must be exhaustive. Add an 'else' branch. When the subject is an enum or a sealed type, you can list every case and leave out else. Then adding a new case to the type breaks every when that doesn't handle it yet, which is exactly the reminder you want.

try works the same way in Kotlin. Its value is the last expression of the try block, or of the catch block that ran:

Java
long cents;
try { cents = Long.parseLong(raw); } catch (NumberFormatException e) { cents = -1; }
Kotlin
val cents = try { raw.toLong() } catch (e: NumberFormatException) { -1 }

Java has no try expression, so you assign in each block or return from each block. (Returning -1 for bad input only keeps the example short. Lesson 7 of this track shows better ways to return a failure.)

You can't write a whole service as expressions, and you shouldn't try. Inside the core, though, expressions push you toward pure code: each line computes one value from the values before it.

try.title: Let the compiler catch the missing branch
steps: Run Expressions (or ExpressionsJava). Check that the statement and expression versions agree for 200, 402 and 503.
In statusOf, delete the else -> line (in Java, the default -> line). Run the demo again and read the compiler error.
Put the line back. In statusStatement, delete the last else status = ... line and run once more. Predict first: will the statement version compile?

code.title: Expressions.kt
code.html: package workbench.functional.l01.demo enum class AuthStatus { APPROVED, DECLINED, ERROR } // Statement style: declare a var, then assign it in every branch and hope you didn't miss one. fun statusStatement(httpCode: Int): AuthStatus { var status: AuthStatus if (httpCode == 200) status = AuthStatus.APPROVED else if (httpCode == 402) status = AuthStatus.DECLINED else status = AuthStatus.ERROR return status } // Expression style: the when IS the value. No var, nothing to forget, nothing to reassign later. fun statusOf(httpCode: Int): AuthStatus = when (httpCode) { 200 -> AuthStatus.APPROVED 402 -> AuthStatus.DECLINED else -> AuthStatus.ERROR } // try is an expression too: the value of the try block, or the value of the catch block. fun parseCents(raw: String): Long = try { raw.toLong() } catch (e: NumberFormatException) { -1 } fun main() { for (code in listOf(200, 402, 503)) { println("$code -> ${statusOf(code)} (statement version: ${statusStatement(code)})") } println("parseCents(\"1250\") = ${parseCents("1250")}") println("parseCents(\"12x\") = ${parseCents("12x")}") }

alt.title: ExpressionsJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.functional.l01.demo; import java.util.List; /** Java twin of Expressions.kt. Java's if and try are statements; the switch expression (JDK 14) is the expression form. */ public class ExpressionsJava { enum AuthStatus { APPROVED, DECLINED, ERROR } // Statement style: declare a variable, then assign it in every branch. static AuthStatus statusStatement(int httpCode) { AuthStatus status; if (httpCode == 200) status = AuthStatus.APPROVED; else if (httpCode == 402) status = AuthStatus.DECLINED; else status = AuthStatus.ERROR; return status; } // Expression style: the switch expression IS the value. static AuthStatus statusOf(int httpCode) { return switch (httpCode) { case 200 -> AuthStatus.APPROVED; case 402 -> AuthStatus.DECLINED; default -> AuthStatus.ERROR; }; } // Java's try is a statement, so the value has to leave through a return in each block. static long parseCents(String raw) { try { return Long.parseLong(raw); } catch (NumberFormatException e) { return -1; } } public static void main(String[] args) { for (int code : List.of(200, 402, 503)) { System.out.println(code + " -> " + statusOf(code) + " (statement version: " + statusStatement(code) + ")"); } System.out.println("parseCents(\"1250\") = " + parseCents("1250")); System.out.println("parseCents(\"12x\") = " + parseCents("12x")); } }

try.expect: Step 2 fails to compile in both languages. Kotlin: 'when' expression must be exhaustive. Add an 'else' branch. javac: the switch expression does not cover all possible input values. Step 3 fails too: Kotlin says variable 'status' must be initialized, javac says variable status might not have been initialized. Both compilers track the missing value either way. The expression form reports it where you made the mistake, and leaves you a val that nobody can reassign afterwards.

sections.html:
A real service can't be pure. It has to read the clock, load rates from the database, write the audit log and call the payout API. Pure functions don't remove those effects. They let you push them to the edges.

The shape has a name, functional core, imperative shell, usually credited to Gary Bernhardt's Destroy All Software screencasts. The core holds the decisions and is pure. The shell does the I/O, and it stays so thin that it has almost no decisions left in it.

For the payout fee, the shell is three steps:

Java
static BigDecimal quotePayoutFee(BigDecimal amount, Clock clock) {
    FeeRates rates = FeeConfig.rates;                  // 1. gather the inputs
    LocalTime now = LocalTime.now(clock);
    BigDecimal fee = payoutFee(amount, rates, now);    // 2. decide, purely
    audit.info(auditLine(amount, fee, now));           // 3. do the effects
    return fee;
}
Kotlin
fun quotePayoutFee(amount: BigDecimal, clock: Clock): BigDecimal {
    val rates = FeeConfig.rates                        // 1. gather the inputs
    val now = LocalTime.now(clock)
    val fee = payoutFee(amount, rates, now)            // 2. decide, purely
    audit.info(auditLine(amount, fee, now))            // 3. do the effects
    return fee
}

Look at auditLine. Deciding what to log is a decision, so it moves into the core as a pure function that returns a String. Writing the line is an effect, so it stays in the shell.

The payoff shows up in where the tests go. The core has all the branches: rounding, the minimum, the cut-off, and later every merchant tier. It gets many fast unit tests with plain values. The shell has no branches, so two tests with Clock.fixed cover it. You still need a fake clock, but in two tests instead of twenty.

This is the target shape for the whole track. Function values, higher-order functions, collection pipelines and errors as values are all tools for making the core bigger and the shell smaller. The last lesson of the track refactors a whole settlement job into this shape.

figure.caption: The shell gathers the inputs, hands them to the pure core as values, and performs whatever the core decided.

analogy: A pure function is a printed fee table taped to the counter. Look up the amount and the time, read off the fee. Two clerks reading the same row get the same number, and reading it changes nothing. The impure version is a clerk who phones head office for today's rate, glances at the wall clock and writes in the ledger every time someone asks. The answer depends on who picked up the phone and when, and asking twice leaves two ledger lines. The analogy breaks in one place: a table can only hold the rows someone printed, while a pure function computes the answer for any amount, to the cent.
world: Temporal already forces this shape on you. Workflow code must be deterministic, so it can't call System.currentTimeMillis() or UUID.randomUUID() directly. The SDK gives you Workflow.currentTimeMillis() and Workflow.randomUUID() instead, and all I/O goes into activities. A workflow that branches on a payout fee is happiest calling a pure payoutFee with the time it got from the SDK. The same split works in a Quarkus REST resource or a Kafka consumer: the resource or the listener gathers the request, the rates and clock.instant(), calls a pure decide(...), and only then writes the row and publishes the event.
mistake: The most common mistake is to think a function became pure because its dependencies are injected. A FeeService(clock, ratesRepo, audit) with a quote(amount) method is testable, but it isn't pure. Each call still reads a clock and a repository and writes a log, so every test needs fakes, and two calls with the same amount can still disagree. Injection moves the hidden inputs into the constructor; it doesn't remove them. Go one step further: let the service gather the inputs and pass them as values to payoutFee(amount, rates, now), and keep the fakes for the two or three tests of the service itself.

compare.title: The same core and shell in Java and Kotlin

java.title: PayoutFees.java
java.html: record FeeRates(BigDecimal percent, BigDecimal minimum, BigDecimal lateSurcharge, LocalTime cutoff) {} final class PayoutFees { // core: static, every input is a parameter, the result is the only output static BigDecimal payoutFee(BigDecimal amount, FeeRates rates, LocalTime requestedAt) { BigDecimal base = amount.multiply(rates.percent()).setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN); BigDecimal atLeastMinimum = base.max(rates.minimum()); return requestedAt.isBefore(rates.cutoff()) ? atLeastMinimum : atLeastMinimum.add(rates.lateSurcharge()); } static String auditLine(BigDecimal amount, BigDecimal fee, LocalTime at) { return "payout fee " + fee + " on " + amount + " at " + at; } // shell: gather, decide, act static BigDecimal quotePayoutFee(BigDecimal amount, Clock clock, Audit audit) { FeeRates rates = FeeConfig.rates; LocalTime now = LocalTime.now(clock); BigDecimal fee = payoutFee(amount, rates, now); audit.write(auditLine(amount, fee, now)); return fee; } }

kotlin.title: PayoutFees.kt
kotlin.html: data class FeeRates(val percent: BigDecimal, val minimum: BigDecimal, val lateSurcharge: BigDecimal, val cutoff: LocalTime) // core: a top-level function, every input is a parameter, the result is the only output fun payoutFee(amount: BigDecimal, rates: FeeRates, requestedAt: LocalTime): BigDecimal { val base = amount.multiply(rates.percent).setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN) val atLeastMinimum = base.max(rates.minimum) return if (requestedAt.isBefore(rates.cutoff)) atLeastMinimum else atLeastMinimum + rates.lateSurcharge } fun auditLine(amount: BigDecimal, fee: BigDecimal, at: LocalTime) = "payout fee $fee on $amount at $at" // shell: gather, decide, act fun quotePayoutFee(amount: BigDecimal, clock: Clock, audit: Audit): BigDecimal { val rates = FeeConfig.rates val now = LocalTime.now(clock) val fee = payoutFee(amount, rates, now) audit.write(auditLine(amount, fee, now)) return fee }

compare.note: The idea is the same in both languages, and so is the risk: neither compiler checks purity, so a Java method or a Kotlin function can call LocalTime.now() and nothing complains. Kotlin makes pure code a little easier to write. val and data classes make values the default, top-level functions need no holder class, and if, when and try produce values, so you rarely need a temporary var. Java gets close with records (JDK 16), switch expressions (JDK 14) and the ternary operator, but if and try stay statements. Kotlin also lets you write + on BigDecimal because the stdlib defines it as an operator for add.

worked.title: Pull a pure refund decision out of a refund handler

steps.say: A refund handler loads the payment, checks two rules and refunds. Before reading on, list every hidden input and every side effect in it.
steps.code: fun refund(paymentId: String) { val payment = repo.load(paymentId) val now = Instant.now() if (payment.status != Status.SETTLED) { log.warn("$paymentId: not settled"); return } if (Duration.between(payment.settledAt, now) > Duration.ofDays(30)) { log.warn("$paymentId: too old"); return } psp.refund(payment.id, payment.amountCents) repo.markRefunded(payment.id) }

alt.html: void refund(String paymentId) { Payment payment = repo.load(paymentId); Instant now = Instant.now(); if (payment.status() != Status.SETTLED) { log.warn(paymentId + ": not settled"); return; } if (Duration.between(payment.settledAt(), now).compareTo(Duration.ofDays(30)) > 0) { log.warn(paymentId + ": too old"); return; } psp.refund(payment.id(), payment.amountCents()); repo.markRefunded(payment.id()); }

steps.say: Hidden inputs: repo.load and Instant.now(). Side effects: two log.warn calls, psp.refund and repo.markRefunded. The decision is tangled with all of them. 1. Give the decision a type, so the core can return it as a value instead of acting on it.
steps.code: sealed interface RefundDecision { data class Refund(val paymentId: String, val amountCents: Long) : RefundDecision data class Reject(val paymentId: String, val reason: String) : RefundDecision }

alt.html: sealed interface RefundDecision { record Refund(String paymentId, long amountCents) implements RefundDecision {} record Reject(String paymentId, String reason) implements RefundDecision {} }

steps.say: 1. Write the core. The payment and the time come in as values, the decision goes out as a value. Self-check: how many tests does it need, and which fakes? (Three, one per branch, and no fakes at all.)
steps.code: fun decideRefund(payment: Payment, now: Instant): RefundDecision = when { payment.status != Status.SETTLED -> RefundDecision.Reject(payment.id, "not settled") Duration.between(payment.settledAt, now) > Duration.ofDays(30) -> RefundDecision.Reject(payment.id, "too old") else -> RefundDecision.Refund(payment.id, payment.amountCents) }

alt.html: static RefundDecision decideRefund(Payment payment, Instant now) { if (payment.status() != Status.SETTLED) return new RefundDecision.Reject(payment.id(), "not settled"); if (Duration.between(payment.settledAt(), now).compareTo(Duration.ofDays(30)) > 0) return new RefundDecision.Reject(payment.id(), "too old"); return new RefundDecision.Refund(payment.id(), payment.amountCents()); }

steps.say: 1. The shell gathers, calls the core and carries out the decision. Its when has no business rules, only one branch per kind of decision, and because RefundDecision is sealed the compiler checks that every kind is handled.
steps.code: fun refund(paymentId: String) { val payment = repo.load(paymentId) // 1. gather when (val d = decideRefund(payment, clock.instant())) { // 2. decide is RefundDecision.Refund -> { // 3. act psp.refund(d.paymentId, d.amountCents) repo.markRefunded(d.paymentId) } is RefundDecision.Reject -> log.warn("${d.paymentId}: ${d.reason}") } }

alt.html: void refund(String paymentId) { Payment payment = repo.load(paymentId); // 1. gather switch (decideRefund(payment, clock.instant())) { // 2. decide case RefundDecision.Refund r -> { // 3. act psp.refund(r.paymentId(), r.amountCents()); repo.markRefunded(r.paymentId()); } case RefundDecision.Reject r -> log.warn(r.paymentId() + ": " + r.reason()); } }

lab.title: Pull the pure fee rule out of quotePayoutFee
steps: Run the tests. Six fail with NotImplementedError. Three already pass: they pin the behaviour of the old quotePayoutFee, which you are about to refactor, and they must stay green.
Write payoutFee from the rules in its KDoc. Use only its three arguments: no FeeConfig, no clock, no AuditLog. Try to write it with vals and one if expression.
Write auditLine. Match the format exactly: payout fee 3.00 on 200.00 at 15:30.
Rewrite the body of quotePayoutFee as a three-step shell: read FeeConfig.rates and the time from clock, call payoutFee, add auditLine(...) to AuditLog.lines, return the fee.
Run the tests until all nine pass. Then open PureFeeTest.kt and notice which tests need the @BeforeEach reset and Clock.fixed. None of the core tests do.
hints: BigDecimal.max(other) returns the larger of the two values, which applies the minimum in one call.
!requestedAt.isBefore(rates.cutoff) is true at the cut-off and after it. requestedAt.isAfter(rates.cutoff) would miss 16:00 exactly, and one test checks that.
43.00 x 0.015 = 0.645. setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN) gives 0.64; HALF_UP would give 0.65 and fail the rounding test.
lab.done: All nine tests in PureFeeTest pass, and quotePayoutFee has no fee arithmetic left in it.

drill.title: Write a core and its shell from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write a pure function lateFee(invoice, today): 5.00 when the invoice is unpaid and today is after its due date, otherwise zero. Then write a shell apply(invoiceId) that loads the invoice, gets today's date from an injected Clock, and saves the fee when there is one. Finally, write one test of the core. Which of the three pieces needs a fake?

answer.html: data class Invoice(val id: String, val dueDate: LocalDate, val paid: Boolean) // core: pure fun lateFee(invoice: Invoice, today: LocalDate): BigDecimal = if (!invoice.paid && today.isAfter(invoice.dueDate)) BigDecimal("5.00") else BigDecimal.ZERO // shell: gather, decide, act class LateFees(private val repo: InvoiceRepo, private val clock: Clock) { fun apply(invoiceId: String) { val invoice = repo.load(invoiceId) val fee = lateFee(invoice, LocalDate.now(clock)) if (fee.signum() > 0) repo.addFee(invoiceId, fee) } } // a core test: no clock, no repository, no reset // assertEquals(BigDecimal("5.00"), lateFee(Invoice("inv_1", LocalDate.of(2026, 3, 1), paid = false), LocalDate.of(2026, 3, 2))) // Only tests of LateFees need a fake repository and Clock.fixed.

alt.html: record Invoice(String id, LocalDate dueDate, boolean paid) {} // core: pure static BigDecimal lateFee(Invoice invoice, LocalDate today) { return !invoice.paid() && today.isAfter(invoice.dueDate()) ? new BigDecimal("5.00") : BigDecimal.ZERO; } // shell: gather, decide, act class LateFees { private final InvoiceRepo repo; private final Clock clock; LateFees(InvoiceRepo repo, Clock clock) { this.repo = repo; this.clock = clock; } void apply(String invoiceId) { Invoice invoice = repo.load(invoiceId); BigDecimal fee = lateFee(invoice, LocalDate.now(clock)); if (fee.signum() > 0) repo.addFee(invoiceId, fee); } } // a core test: no clock, no repository, no reset // assertEquals(new BigDecimal("5.00"), lateFee(new Invoice("inv_1", LocalDate.of(2026, 3, 1), false), LocalDate.of(2026, 3, 2)));

recap: A pure function's result depends only on its arguments, and calling it changes nothing outside it.
Hidden inputs (the clock, Random, a mutable global) break purity just as side effects (I/O, logging, mutation) do.
Referential transparency: a pure call can be replaced by its value. Only then are extract, inline, cache, retry and parallel calls safe without reading the body.
In Kotlin, if, when and try are expressions. Compute a val from them instead of assigning a var in branches.
Functional core, imperative shell: decisions in pure functions with many plain-value tests, I/O in a thin shell with a few.

explain.prompt: A teammate says: "quotePayoutFee is already testable, we inject a Clock." In your own words, explain why pulling out payoutFee(amount, rates, requestedAt) is still worth doing.
explain.answer: Injecting a Clock makes the time controllable, but quotePayoutFee still has other hidden inputs and effects. It reads the global rates, so every test has to reset them or depend on test order, and it writes an audit line, so tests have to capture or ignore the log. Each test of a rule also needs a fixed clock built just right. If I pull the rule into payoutFee(amount, rates, requestedAt), every input is a parameter and the fee is the only output. I can test each rule in one line with plain values, in any order, on any number of threads. The old function becomes a three-step shell (read, decide, write), and two tests with Clock.fixed are enough for it.

deeper.html:
Purity has fuzzy edges, and it helps to know where they are.

Allocation is a change to the heap, but nobody calls a function impure because it creates a BigDecimal. What counts is whether a caller can observe the change. The same goes for a cache inside a function: memoize in lesson 3 stores results in a map, yet from the outside the function still returns the same answer for the same arguments, so callers can treat it as pure.

Throwing is the contested case. require(amount.signum() > 0) makes a function partial: it has no answer for some inputs. Many people still call it pure, because the same bad input always throws the same way. What hurts is using exceptions for expected outcomes, like a declined card, because the signature no longer tells you what can come back. Lesson 7 of this track returns those outcomes as values.

Kotlin can't check purity, but it can catch the most common bug with pure functions: calling one and dropping the result. Compile with -Xreturn-value-checker=full and Kotlin 2.4.21 warns on a call like withFee(amountCents, 300) on a line of its own:

Java
static long withFee(long amountCents, long feeCents) { return amountCents + feeCents; }

static long total(long amountCents) {
    withFee(amountCents, 300);    // javac says nothing
    return amountCents;
}
Kotlin
fun withFee(amountCents: Long, feeCents: Long): Long = amountCents + feeCents

fun total(amountCents: Long): Long {
    withFee(amountCents, 300)     // warning: unused return value of 'withFee'.
    return amountCents
}

In a quick test the warning covered Kotlin functions, including stdlib ones like map, but not Java methods: a dropped amount.add(fee) on a BigDecimal got no warning. That one stays a code-review catch.
